newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia prepared to recognise Caspian oilfields.
newsitem.headline: Russia prepared to recognise Caspian oilfields.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Tuesday said his country was ready to recognise the oilfields of neighbouring states outside a 45-mile (72 km) coastal zone in the Caspian Sea.

"Russia is ready to recognise the jurisdiction of Caspian states not only in the coastal zones but also in relation to oilfields situated outside those zones," Primakov told a news conference in the Turkmen capital Ashgabat.
Russia had previously argued that the sea was a lake whose resources should be developed and shared equally by all the littoral states -- Russia, Iran, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.

Primakov was speaking after meeting the foreign ministers of Iran, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan to thrash out the legal status of the Caspian Sea which was divided up between the Soviet Union and Iran first in 1921 and again in 1940.
But since the break up of the Soviet Union the Caspian has become the subject of an intense diplomatic and legal battle over the body of water's immense reserves of oil and gas.

The focus of the present battle rages over whether the Caspian is a sea or a lake. Academics argue the sea is actually a salt-water lake but the control of billions of dollars worth of black gold ride on the apparently arcane question.

The Caspian ranks eighth in the world in terms of discovered oil reserves. Reserves in Kazakhstan's continental shelf of the Caspian alone are 10 billion tonnes. The sea has not been fully studied and may hold much more.
No agreement was reached at the meeting on the Caspian Sea's status but a Turkmen foreign ministry spokesman said the five countries would meet again to discuss the issue in Kazakhstan in December.
